transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, nice to meet you too. I guess I’m here because... well, for almost two years now, I haven't been able to shake this absolute certainty that ever since my big commission, a few people in the ensemble have been quietly undermining my work. It’s always subtle things, you know? Sudden schedule changes, weird seating choices, these little pointed comments during rehearsals. And they’ll show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away, but I know what's really happening. 

Which is funny, actually, because emails have been a total mess for the group lately anyway. Our server migrated last month and I lost half my inbox. Do you use Outlook? I swear, every time they do an update, they move the search bar and it takes me ten minutes just to find a message from the brass section. I actually missed a dentist appointment last week because the reminder went straight to my spam folder, and my dentist was so annoyed. He collects vintage metronomes, actually, which is a weird coincidence for me, but he has this one from the 1800s sitting right by the chair. 

But, um, anyway... yeah, the ensemble situation. It's just been really stressful dealing with them, so I figured I should probably talk to someone about it.
Has anyone else independently confirmed that these ensemble members are deliberately trying to undermine you?

Confirmed it? Well... no, not exactly in so many words. Because, like I was saying, it’s been almost two years since the commission, and I just have this absolute certainty that they are quietly undermining my work. They’re smart about it, you know? They use the sudden schedule changes and the weird seating choices, and whenever I try to point it out to someone else in the group, the people doing it just pull out those same emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away. So everyone else just looks at the notes and believes them. 

Speaking of notes, actually, we switched to using iPads for our sheet music this season. It's supposed to save paper, which is great, but the glare from the stage lights is just terrible. We played at this historic theater downtown last weekend—beautiful acoustics, built in like 1924, I think—and the lighting guy absolutely refused to dim the overheads. I had to order one of those matte screen protectors online, but I could not get the air bubbles out of the corners. Have you ever tried putting one of those on a large tablet? It is literally impossible to keep the dust out. I spent like twenty minutes in my bathroom with the shower running just to get the steam to settle the dust, and it still didn't work perfectly. 

But, um... wait, what were you asking me? Oh, right, if anyone else sees them doing it. Yeah, no, they just look at the schedule emails and tell me it's just normal administrative stuff.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

Voices? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. No voices or anything. Although, speaking of hearing things, my neighbor just bought this wind chime. It's one of those massive, heavy metal ones, you know? The tubes are like two feet long. And they hung it right outside my bedroom window. Every time the wind picks up, it sounds like a cathedral bell going off. I mean, I appreciate good resonance as much as the next guy, but at 3:00 AM, it's a bit much. 

I actually tried to buy them a smaller, wooden one as a sort of passive-aggressive gift, but the hardware store down the street was closed for renovation. They’re putting in this new coffee shop attached to it, which is weird, right? Coffee and power tools. Seems like a liability waiting to happen. I used an angle grinder once for a sound art installation I was working on in grad school, and even with the safety goggles, I was terrified. The sparks flew everywhere, and I ended up singing the sleeve of my favorite sweater. It was this really nice merino wool one my sister got me in Ireland. 

But, uh... no, to answer your question, I don't hear any voices. Just the wind chimes. And the occasional siren, since I live pretty close to the hospital.
Have there been times when you felt unusually energized or euphoric for days at a time?

Energized or euphoric? Um, no. I don't think so. I mean, I get excited when a piece comes together, but not for days at a time. I usually just feel tired, honestly. 

Especially with this new espresso machine I got. It’s one of those manual lever ones, you know? Beautiful piece of machinery, Italian made, lots of chrome. But pulling a shot takes so much physical effort, and half the time I don't grind the beans fine enough, so it just gushes out and tastes sour. I’ve been buying beans from this local roaster who supposedly sources directly from farms in Colombia, but honestly, I think they roast them too light. The bags have these really intricate illustrations on them, though—like, line drawings of toucans and jaguars. 

My cousin used to draw like that. She went to art school in Chicago and then ended up doing graphic design for a dog food company. It’s funny how that happens, right? You study fine art and then you’re designing kibble bags. She has a golden retriever that sheds constantly. I visited her last Thanksgiving and I swear I was picking blonde hairs off my black slacks for a week. 

But, uh, anyway... no, no unusual energy or euphoria or anything like that. Just regular tired.
Outside of this issue with the ensemble, have you had any other beliefs that people would say are strange or hard to believe?

Strange beliefs? No, I don't think so. I mean, outside of what's happening with the ensemble, everything else is just... normal. 

Although, speaking of strange things, I did see the weirdest documentary the other night. It was about these deep-sea tube worms that live near hydrothermal vents. They don't even have a digestive system, they just rely on this symbiotic bacteria to turn the toxic chemicals into food. It’s absolutely fascinating how life adapts to such extreme pressure and darkness. It made me want to write a piece based on that environment, you know? Something really low and rumbling, maybe using a contrabassoon and some heavy synth drones. 

I actually looked up the price of a decent analog synthesizer, and they are ridiculously expensive. Even the used ones on Reverb are going for thousands. I guess there’s this huge vintage revival happening right now, kind of like how everyone is buying vinyl records again. My dad still has his original pressing of Abbey Road, but he keeps it in the basement where it’s totally damp. I keep telling him he needs a dehumidifier down there, or the sleeve is going to get completely ruined by mildew. He just brushes me off, though. He’s always been stubborn like that, especially when it comes to his old stuff. 

But, wait... what did you ask? Oh, right, other strange beliefs. No, definitely not. Just the ensemble stuff. That's the only thing.
Do people often tell you that your speech goes off track or is hard to follow?

Hard to follow? Off track? I don't think people say that. I mean, I think I communicate pretty clearly. I'm used to directing musicians, right? You have to be precise when you're explaining how you want a phrase articulated. If you want it detached but not quite staccato, you have to find the right words. 

Like this cellist I worked with last month. He was incredibly talented, technically flawless, but he played everything so aggressively. I had to spend like twenty minutes explaining the concept of a 'whispered' tone to him. We ended up using this special rosin on his bow—it was this dark amber stuff from France, supposedly made using a recipe from the 1800s. It smelled amazing, kind of like pine needles and old books. I actually bought a candle that was supposed to smell like old books once, but it just smelled like vanilla and dust. I got it at this little boutique downtown that sells all these imported soaps and artisanal honey. The honey was good, though. I put it in my tea when I get a sore throat, especially during the winter when the heating in my apartment dries out the air. The radiators are ancient and they clank so loudly. 

But, uh, no... people don't usually say I'm hard to follow. I think I make sense.
Has your work or day-to-day functioning gotten noticeably worse since this started?

Worse? I mean, not drastically. The main thing is that rehearsals and, you know, professional emails just take a lot more energy now. I find myself rereading my decisions or asking for extra clarification from the musicians just to be absolutely sure. But I haven't lost any work, and I'm still taking care of myself. 

Speaking of taking care of myself, I actually started trying to make my own sourdough bread last week. Everyone says it’s so relaxing, but keeping the starter alive is like having a pet. You have to feed it at the exact right time or it gets this weird liquid on top called 'hooch.' I used this organic rye flour I found at the farmers market. The market was packed, by the way. I ended up buying these heirloom tomatoes that were purple and green. They looked amazing, but when I sliced them up for a sandwich, they were completely mealy inside. There's nothing worse than a mealy tomato, right? It ruins the whole texture. I had to throw the whole sandwich out and just eat a bowl of cereal instead. I buy that brand with the little dried strawberries in it, but they always sink to the bottom of the bag so the last bowl is just overwhelmingly fruity. 

But, um... yeah, to answer your question, my day-to-day is mostly fine. Just a bit more exhausting with the extra checking.
Before all this started, had you had any significant medical or neurological illness?

Medical issues? Like before all this? No, I've always been pretty healthy. Never had anything major like that. 

I did break my wrist once when I was a kid, though. I was trying to ride my bike down this steep hill near my house, and I completely wiped out on some loose gravel. The cast was so itchy, especially during the summer. We went to the beach that year, and I couldn't even go in the water. I just sat on the sand under an umbrella reading these old sci-fi paperbacks my uncle gave me. He had this massive collection of Isaac Asimov and Arthur C. Clarke. The covers always had those amazing, retro-futuristic paintings on them, you know? The ones with the giant geometric spaceships and the weirdly colored planets. I actually tried to find some of those specific editions online a while back, just for nostalgia. Turns out they're actually worth a bit of money now if they're in good condition. Most of the ones I found had completely yellowed pages, though. Old paper gets that distinct smell, kind of sweet and musty. 

But, uh, anyway... no, no major medical or neurological stuff. Just the broken wrist when I was little.
Do you think it is at all possible that you could be mistaken about the ensemble members undermining you?

Mistaken? I... I don't see how I could be. I mean, that's why I'm here, right? Because for almost two years now, I haven't been able to shake this absolute certainty about it. Ever since that big commission, a few of them have been doing it. Just quietly undermining my work. It's the schedule changes, the seating choices, the little comments during rehearsals. And I know they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away, but it doesn't change what I know is happening. 

It's like when you're tuning an orchestra, you know? The oboe plays the A, and everyone else is supposed to match it. But sometimes the strings will be just a fraction of a cent flat. Not enough for a casual listener to notice, but if you have a trained ear, it drives you absolutely crazy. It creates this subtle dissonance that just hangs in the air. I actually bought a new digital tuner last month because I thought my old one was losing its calibration. It's one of those strobe tuners, really precise. I ordered it from this specialty music shop in Chicago. I went to Chicago once for a conference, right in the middle of winter. The wind coming off Lake Michigan is no joke. I had to buy a new coat while I was there because the one I brought was completely useless. It was this heavy wool peacoat, navy blue. I still have it in my closet, actually, but I never wear it because it weighs like ten pounds and the buttons are loose. I tried to sew one back on, but I used the wrong color thread, so now it looks a bit ridiculous. 

But, um, anyway... no, I'm not mistaken. I know what they're doing, even if they try to cover it up with their little explanations.
Has anything about what these ensemble members are doing seemed impossible by ordinary means, like influencing you in ways normal people couldn't?

Impossible by ordinary means? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, they're just musicians, right? They're not doing anything supernatural or... or reading my mind. It's just normal, everyday sabotage. Missing cues, changing schedules, that kind of thing. 

Speaking of schedules, I actually bought a new planner recently to try and keep everything straight. It's one of those really nice leather-bound ones, you know? With the thick paper that doesn't bleed through when you use a fountain pen. I love fountain pens. I have this vintage Parker 51 that I found at an estate sale a few years ago. It took me forever to figure out how to clean the old dried ink out of the aerometric filler. I ended up watching like, three hours of YouTube tutorials on pen restoration. There's this whole community of people who just restore old pens. One guy had this amazing video where he fixed a cracked celluloid barrel using some kind of solvent welding technique. It was fascinating. I actually tried to buy some of the solvent he used, but you can't get it shipped to residential addresses anymore because it's apparently highly flammable. Probably for the best, honestly. I'd probably end up melting the pen entirely or setting my desk on fire. My desk is this old oak roll-top that I got from my grandfather, so I'd hate to ruin it. It has all these tiny little cubby holes that are completely useless for modern things, but they look great. 

But, uh, no... to answer your question, they aren't doing anything impossible. Just normal, frustrating things to undermine me.
Have you noticed yourself becoming much less interested in people or activities you used to enjoy?

Less interested? No, I don't think so. I mean, I still love music, obviously. I'm still composing, still trying to get my work out there despite... well, despite everything. I still enjoy reading, too. I just finished this incredible biography of Mahler. 

It's actually a really heavy book, physically, I mean. Hardcover, almost a thousand pages. I usually prefer reading on my tablet because it's easier to hold when I'm lying in bed, but the screen glare was starting to give me headaches. I went to the optometrist a few weeks ago to see if I needed a new prescription, but he said my eyes are fine. He suggested I try those blue-light blocking glasses. I bought a pair online, but they have these really thick, tortoiseshell frames that make me look like a 1950s librarian. I wore them to the grocery store once and the cashier kept giving me these weird looks. Or maybe it was because I bought like, six jars of artichoke hearts. They were on sale, and I was going to make this Mediterranean pasta salad I saw on a cooking show. The host of the show was this really energetic Italian guy who kept shouting at the camera. He made it look so easy, but when I tried it, the dressing split and it just looked like an oily mess. I ended up eating it anyway because I didn't want to waste the artichokes. They're surprisingly expensive when they're not on sale. 

But, um, anyway... no, I haven't lost interest in things. I still enjoy my usual hobbies and everything.
During these past two years, have you had a period when you felt very depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Depressed? No, no, I haven't had anything like that. I mean, I get frustrated with the ensemble, obviously, but not depressed. I don't really get down like that. Well, maybe a little gloomy when it rains for days on end, but that's just the weather. 

Actually, the last time it rained really heavily, my ceiling started leaking right over my piano. It's just a Yamaha upright, but I love the action on the keys. I had to scramble to put this orange plastic bucket on top of it to catch the water. The funny thing is, the sound of the water hitting the bottom of the bucket was pitching a perfect B-flat. Just... drip, drip, B-flat, B-flat. I actually pulled out my phone and recorded it to see if I could sample it for a piece I was working on. I use Logic Pro for my mixing, mostly. A lot of my friends swear by Ableton, but I just can't get used to the interface. It feels too blocky to me. I watched this masterclass by Hans Zimmer recently where he showed off his studio, and it is just wall-to-wall modular synthesizers. It looks like the bridge of a spaceship. I'd love to have a setup like that, but my apartment barely has enough room for a decent dining table. I usually end up eating dinner on my couch while watching nature documentaries. I saw this amazing one about cephalopods the other night. Did you know octopuses have three hearts? It's wild. They pump blue blood, too, because it's copper-based instead of iron. 

But, um... sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, feeling depressed. No, no periods of depression for me.
Have other people ever said that your thoughts seem jumbled or that you jump from one idea to another in a way that is hard to follow?

Jumbled? No, I don't think anyone has ever told me that. I mean, my musicians complain about a lot of things, but usually it's about my tempos or the rehearsal schedule, not that I'm hard to follow. 

Speaking of rehearsal schedules, I was trying to coordinate a string quartet practice last week, and trying to get four musicians in the same room at the same time is like herding cats. I had to use this online scheduling poll thing, Doodle, I think it's called? But the cellist, David, he completely ignored it and just texted me a list of times he *couldn't* do, which is entirely unhelpful. David is a great player, don't get me wrong. He has this beautiful 19th-century French cello that just sings in the upper register. He bought it at an auction in Paris a few years ago. I've always wanted to go to Paris. I had a layover at Charles de Gaulle once, but I don't think that counts. The airport there is huge and confusing, honestly. I almost missed my connection to Berlin because I couldn't figure out which terminal I was supposed to be in. The signage was terrible, or maybe I was just sleep-deprived. I always get terrible jet lag when I fly east. I read somewhere that taking melatonin can help, but last time I tried it, I just had these incredibly vivid dreams about being trapped in a giant hourglass. Sand getting everywhere. It was awful. I ended up waking up at 3 AM and just eating cold pizza in my hotel room. 

But, uh, no, nobody's ever said my thoughts are jumbled. I think I'm pretty clear when I speak.
Has anyone ever told you that, when you talk, you go off on tangents or lose track of the question?

Go off on tangents? Lose track of the question? No, I don't think anyone's ever said that. I mean, I'm a director, I have to be pretty focused to keep everyone on the same page. 

Although, keeping people on the same page is literally impossible with sheet music these days. Half the ensemble uses iPads now, and they all have these Bluetooth page-turning pedals. It's supposed to be seamless, but during our last run-through, the second violinist's pedal disconnected right in the middle of a tricky allegro section. He had to stop playing to swipe the screen, and it totally ruined the momentum. I told him he should just go back to paper, but he says paper is bad for the environment. Which I get, I try to recycle as much as I can. I actually started composting recently, too. I got this little bin for my kitchen counter. It's supposed to be odor-free, but I put some onion skins in there last week and the whole apartment smelled like a deli for two days. I ended up having to buy this expensive citrus room spray to cover it up. The bottle said it was made with essential oils from the Amalfi coast. I love the smell of citrus, especially grapefruit. Have you ever tried a grapefruit brûlée? You cut it in half, sprinkle some sugar on top, and use a blowtorch to caramelize it. It's incredible. I got a kitchen torch for Christmas last year from my sister. She's a pastry chef in Chicago. Chicago is great, but the winters are just brutal. The wind off the lake goes right through your coat. 

But, um... wait, what were you asking about? Oh, tangents. No, no one's ever told me I do that. I usually get right to the point.
Have you been avoiding other people more than usual?

Avoiding people? No, not really. I mean, I have to be around people all the time for work. Rehearsals, meetings with venue managers, all that stuff. It's actually exhausting sometimes. 

Like yesterday, I had to meet with the lighting director for our upcoming performance at this old theater downtown. The place is gorgeous, all this ornate gold leafing and red velvet everywhere. It feels like stepping back into the 1920s. But the lighting rig is an absolute nightmare. It's half digital, half analog, and the guy running it kept complaining about the power draw. He was wearing this vintage leather jacket that squeaked every time he moved his arms. It was so distracting. I used to have a leather jacket like that in college, but I accidentally left it at a diner in Boston. We had gone there after a concert, and I ordered this massive plate of blueberry pancakes. Best pancakes I've ever had. I think the secret is they put a little bit of lemon zest in the batter. I tried making them at home once, but I totally messed up the ratio of baking powder and they came out flat as crepes. Crepes are good too, though, especially with Nutella and strawberries. I went to a crepe stand in Montreal once, and the guy making them was juggling the spatulas. It was like dinner and a show. 

But, uh, avoiding people? No, I'm pretty social. I don't really hide away or anything.
Can you tell me, in one sentence, why you think those ensemble members are undermining you?

Well, you see, I'm here because for almost two years I've been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it. 

Which reminds me of this one email chain we had about the seating arrangement for the cellos. It was a complete disaster. The first chair cellist, Sarah, she insisted on being closer to the violas, saying it helped her hear the inner harmonies better. But I know she just wanted to be further away from the air conditioning vent. Those vents in the rehearsal hall are so loud, they sound like a jet engine taking off. Speaking of jet engines, I was watching this documentary the other day about how they test those things. They literally shoot frozen chickens into the turbines to simulate bird strikes. It's wild. I can't imagine being the person whose job it is to buy frozen chickens for that. Do they just go to a regular grocery store? I went to the store yesterday to get some chicken, actually, but they were completely out of thighs, which are the best part for roasting. I ended up getting breasts instead, but they always dry out so fast unless you brine them first. I have this great brine recipe with peppercorns and bay leaves. Bay leaves are funny, aren't they? You put them in, but you're not supposed to eat them. It feels like a trick. 

But anyway, yeah, that's why I think they're undermining me.
Have you ever felt that your thoughts were being controlled by someone else?

Controlled by someone else? Like mind control? No, I've never felt anything like that. My thoughts are my own. 

Though, sometimes I wish someone else could take over my thoughts just so I could get a break, you know? Especially when I'm trying to figure out the pacing for a new piece. I'll just lie in bed staring at the ceiling, trying to hear the transition from the woodwinds to the brass, and my brain just won't shut off. Speaking of brass, I had to take my French horn in for a cleaning last month. It's a vintage Conn 8D, beautiful instrument, but the valves get sticky if you don't oil them religiously. The repair guy I go to is this older gentleman who works out of his garage. His garage is amazing, it's packed floor to ceiling with instrument parts and old radios. He actually fixes antique radios as a hobby. He showed me this one from the 1930s that he restored, it had this gorgeous wooden cabinet with a glowing dial. It made me want to start listening to those old radio dramas, like The Shadow or something. I tried listening to a podcast once that was styled like an old radio show, but the voice acting was just so over the top I couldn't get into it. I mostly just listen to audiobooks now when I'm driving. I'm on this huge sci-fi kick right now. I just finished this book about a colony on Mars where they have to farm potatoes in their own... well, you know. It's fascinating how much science goes into making those stories believable. 

But no, my thoughts are definitely my own. No one's controlling them.
Have you ever believed that ordinary events, comments, or messages were meant specifically for you?

Meant specifically for me? Like hidden messages? No, I don't really think like that. I mean, I read reviews of our performances, and sometimes it feels like a critic is taking a personal swipe at my tempo choices, but that's just normal criticism, right? 

Speaking of reviews, there's this one local arts blogger who always has something to say about the percussion section. He's obsessed with the timpani. I actually ran into him at a coffee shop a few weeks ago. He was ordering this incredibly complicated matcha latte with oat milk and two pumps of vanilla. I don't get the whole matcha craze, honestly. It tastes like grass clippings to me. I prefer just a straight black coffee, maybe an espresso if I'm really dragging. I bought an espresso machine for my apartment last year, one of those shiny Italian ones. It took me a solid month to figure out how to pull a decent shot without burning the beans. You have to get the grind size exactly right, and the tamp pressure... it's practically a science experiment every morning. My neighbor actually complained about the noise of the grinder once. She's this sweet older lady who knits these tiny sweaters for her Chihuahua. The dog's name is Barnaby, and he barks at literally everything. A leaf blows across the sidewalk? Barnaby loses his mind. It's kind of hilarious, but also a little annoying when I'm trying to write a score. 

But yeah, no, I don't think random things are secretly meant for me. Just normal stuff.
Do your thoughts ever suddenly stop in the middle, as if your mind goes blank?

Stop in the middle? Like going completely blank? No, I haven't noticed anything like that. My brain is usually going a mile a minute, honestly. 

Though, I do get writer's block sometimes when I'm staring at a blank score. It's the absolute worst feeling, just looking at the empty staff paper. I actually have to use a very specific type of staff paper, it has to be this slightly off-white, almost cream color, because the bright white glares way too much under my desk lamp. My desk lamp is one of those vintage architect lamps with the adjustable spring arms. I found it at a thrift store for like ten bucks. It was a total steal, but I had to rewire the whole thing myself because the original cord was completely frayed and I really didn't want to start a fire. Speaking of fires, the fire alarm in my apartment building went off at 3 AM on Tuesday. Turns out someone on the fourth floor fell asleep while boiling eggs. Who boils eggs at 3 AM? And how do you even burn boiled eggs? All the water has to evaporate first. I usually soft-boil mine for exactly six and a half minutes, then drop them straight into an ice bath. It makes the shells peel off so easily. 

But anyway, what were we... oh, right. No, my thoughts don't just stop or go blank.
Have you ever seen things that other people could not see?

Seen things? You mean like hallucinations or something? No, definitely not. I've got pretty good eyesight, actually. 

Though I did have to get new glasses a couple of months ago. My prescription barely changed, but I sat on my old frames by accident. I was in a rush to get to rehearsal and just flopped down on the couch without looking. They were these great tortoiseshell frames, too. I ended up getting wire-rimmed ones this time, kind of a retro look. The optometrist was this guy who wouldn't stop talking about his trip to Iceland. He spent like twenty minutes telling me about the hot springs and the puffins while he was shining that bright light in my eyes. I'd love to go to Iceland someday, maybe record some ambient soundscapes near the glaciers. I've been experimenting a lot with field recordings lately. I bought this portable Zoom recorder, and I just take it on walks and record random stuff—traffic, birds, the subway doors closing. I actually used a sample of a subway train braking in this experimental piece I wrote for a string quartet. The cellist hated it, she said it was too jarring, but that was exactly the point. I'm trying to push boundaries, you know? The classical music scene can be so rigid sometimes. If you don't write exactly like Mahler or Shostakovich, people look at you funny. I went to this concert last week where they played a piece entirely composed of silence and occasional coughing. It was... an experience. 

But no, I don't see things that aren't there. My vision is perfectly normal.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the belief is a fixed delusion or could be grounded in objectively verifiable events by testing for external corroboration.
doctor.question: Has anyone else independently confirmed that these ensemble members are deliberately trying to undermine you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for almost two years I’ve been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if anyone else has confirmed the patient's belief that the ensemble members are undermining him, which is directly related to the fixed, unshakeable nature of the belief despite lack of external confirmation or contradictory evidence (the core of the delusion).

patient.answer:
Confirmed it? Well... no, not exactly in so many words. Because, like I was saying, it’s been almost two years since the commission, and I just have this absolute certainty that they are quietly undermining my work. They’re smart about it, you know? They use the sudden schedule changes and the weird seating choices, and whenever I try to point it out to someone else in the group, the people doing it just pull out those same emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away. So everyone else just looks at the notes and believes them. 

Speaking of notes, actually, we switched to using iPads for our sheet music this season. It's supposed to save paper, which is great, but the glare from the stage lights is just terrible. We played at this historic theater downtown last weekend—beautiful acoustics, built in like 1924, I think—and the lighting guy absolutely refused to dim the overheads. I had to order one of those matte screen protectors online, but I could not get the air bubbles out of the corners. Have you ever tried putting one of those on a large tablet? It is literally impossible to keep the dust out. I spent like twenty minutes in my bathroom with the shower running just to get the steam to settle the dust, and it still didn't work perfectly. 

But, um... wait, what were you asking me? Oh, right, if anyone else sees them doing it. Yeah, no, they just look at the schedule emails and tell me it's just normal administrative stuff.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic belief is accompanied by hallucinations, which would help distinguish delusional disorder/paranoid personality from schizophrenia spectrum or organic psychosis.
doctor.question: Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about auditory hallucinations (hearing voices), which is not covered by any of my symptom profiles (Delusions, Additional Requirement 1, Functional Impairment, Duration).

patient.answer:
Voices? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. No voices or anything. Although, speaking of hearing things, my neighbor just bought this wind chime. It's one of those massive, heavy metal ones, you know? The tubes are like two feet long. And they hung it right outside my bedroom window. Every time the wind picks up, it sounds like a cathedral bell going off. I mean, I appreciate good resonance as much as the next guy, but at 3:00 AM, it's a bit much. 

I actually tried to buy them a smaller, wooden one as a sort of passive-aggressive gift, but the hardware store down the street was closed for renovation. They’re putting in this new coffee shop attached to it, which is weird, right? Coffee and power tools. Seems like a liability waiting to happen. I used an angle grinder once for a sound art installation I was working on in grad school, and even with the safety goggles, I was terrified. The sparks flew everywhere, and I ended up singing the sleeve of my favorite sweater. It was this really nice merino wool one my sister got me in Ireland. 

But, uh... no, to answer your question, I don't hear any voices. Just the wind chimes. And the occasional siren, since I live pretty close to the hospital.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been prominent mood episodes, especially mania, to distinguish a delusional/psychotic disorder from schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: Have there been times when you felt unusually energized or euphoric for days at a time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of mania (feeling unusually energized or euphoric for days at a time), which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Energized or euphoric? Um, no. I don't think so. I mean, I get excited when a piece comes together, but not for days at a time. I usually just feel tired, honestly. 

Especially with this new espresso machine I got. It’s one of those manual lever ones, you know? Beautiful piece of machinery, Italian made, lots of chrome. But pulling a shot takes so much physical effort, and half the time I don't grind the beans fine enough, so it just gushes out and tastes sour. I’ve been buying beans from this local roaster who supposedly sources directly from farms in Colombia, but honestly, I think they roast them too light. The bags have these really intricate illustrations on them, though—like, line drawings of toucans and jaguars. 

My cousin used to draw like that. She went to art school in Chicago and then ended up doing graphic design for a dog food company. It’s funny how that happens, right? You study fine art and then you’re designing kibble bags. She has a golden retriever that sheds constantly. I visited her last Thanksgiving and I swear I was picking blonde hairs off my black slacks for a week. 

But, uh, anyway... no, no unusual energy or euphoria or anything like that. Just regular tired.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the belief is confined to a single persecutory delusion or accompanied by broader psychotic disorganization, which helps distinguish delusional disorder/paranoid personality from schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.
doctor.question: Outside of this issue with the ensemble, have you had any other beliefs that people would say are strange or hard to believe?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the presence of other strange or bizarre beliefs (delusions) outside of the main issue with the ensemble. My symptom profile covers the specific delusion about the ensemble, functional impairment, and duration, but does not explicitly address whether I have *other* bizarre beliefs.

patient.answer:
Strange beliefs? No, I don't think so. I mean, outside of what's happening with the ensemble, everything else is just... normal. 

Although, speaking of strange things, I did see the weirdest documentary the other night. It was about these deep-sea tube worms that live near hydrothermal vents. They don't even have a digestive system, they just rely on this symbiotic bacteria to turn the toxic chemicals into food. It’s absolutely fascinating how life adapts to such extreme pressure and darkness. It made me want to write a piece based on that environment, you know? Something really low and rumbling, maybe using a contrabassoon and some heavy synth drones. 

I actually looked up the price of a decent analog synthesizer, and they are ridiculously expensive. Even the used ones on Reverb are going for thousands. I guess there’s this huge vintage revival happening right now, kind of like how everyone is buying vinyl records again. My dad still has his original pressing of Abbey Road, but he keeps it in the basement where it’s totally damp. I keep telling him he needs a dehumidifier down there, or the sleeve is going to get completely ruined by mildew. He just brushes me off, though. He’s always been stubborn like that, especially when it comes to his old stuff. 

But, wait... what did you ask? Oh, right, other strange beliefs. No, definitely not. Just the ensemble stuff. That's the only thing.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is prominent formal thought disorder/disorganized speech, which would help distinguish schizophrenia spectrum disorders from a persistent delusional disorder or paranoid personality pattern.
doctor.question: Do people often tell you that your speech goes off track or is hard to follow?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about disorganized speech (going off track or being hard to follow), which is a symptom of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders (derailment/loose associations). This is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Hard to follow? Off track? I don't think people say that. I mean, I think I communicate pretty clearly. I'm used to directing musicians, right? You have to be precise when you're explaining how you want a phrase articulated. If you want it detached but not quite staccato, you have to find the right words. 

Like this cellist I worked with last month. He was incredibly talented, technically flawless, but he played everything so aggressively. I had to spend like twenty minutes explaining the concept of a 'whispered' tone to him. We ended up using this special rosin on his bow—it was this dark amber stuff from France, supposedly made using a recipe from the 1800s. It smelled amazing, kind of like pine needles and old books. I actually bought a candle that was supposed to smell like old books once, but it just smelled like vanilla and dust. I got it at this little boutique downtown that sells all these imported soaps and artisanal honey. The honey was good, though. I put it in my tea when I get a sore throat, especially during the winter when the heating in my apartment dries out the air. The radiators are ancient and they clank so loudly. 

But, uh, no... people don't usually say I'm hard to follow. I think I make sense.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there has been a prominent decline in functioning outside the delusional belief, which helps distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum conditions.
doctor.question: Has your work or day-to-day functioning gotten noticeably worse since this started?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: The main consequence is that rehearsals and professional emails take more energy because I reread decisions and sometimes ask for extra clarification, but I haven’t lost work or stopped taking care of myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if my work or day-to-day functioning has gotten noticeably worse since this started, which directly corresponds to the functional impairment symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Worse? I mean, not drastically. The main thing is that rehearsals and, you know, professional emails just take a lot more energy now. I find myself rereading my decisions or asking for extra clarification from the musicians just to be absolutely sure. But I haven't lost any work, and I'm still taking care of myself. 

Speaking of taking care of myself, I actually started trying to make my own sourdough bread last week. Everyone says it’s so relaxing, but keeping the starter alive is like having a pet. You have to feed it at the exact right time or it gets this weird liquid on top called 'hooch.' I used this organic rye flour I found at the farmers market. The market was packed, by the way. I ended up buying these heirloom tomatoes that were purple and green. They looked amazing, but when I sliced them up for a sandwich, they were completely mealy inside. There's nothing worse than a mealy tomato, right? It ruins the whole texture. I had to throw the whole sandwich out and just eat a bowl of cereal instead. I buy that brand with the little dried strawberries in it, but they always sink to the bottom of the bag so the last bowl is just overwhelmingly fruity. 

But, um... yeah, to answer your question, my day-to-day is mostly fine. Just a bit more exhausting with the extra checking.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are due to a medical or neurological condition, which would separate organic psychosis (F06.2) from primary psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Before all this started, had you had any significant medical or neurological illness?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about significant medical or neurological illness before the onset of the current symptoms, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Medical issues? Like before all this? No, I've always been pretty healthy. Never had anything major like that. 

I did break my wrist once when I was a kid, though. I was trying to ride my bike down this steep hill near my house, and I completely wiped out on some loose gravel. The cast was so itchy, especially during the summer. We went to the beach that year, and I couldn't even go in the water. I just sat on the sand under an umbrella reading these old sci-fi paperbacks my uncle gave me. He had this massive collection of Isaac Asimov and Arthur C. Clarke. The covers always had those amazing, retro-futuristic paintings on them, you know? The ones with the giant geometric spaceships and the weirdly colored planets. I actually tried to find some of those specific editions online a while back, just for nostalgia. Turns out they're actually worth a bit of money now if they're in good condition. Most of the ones I found had completely yellowed pages, though. Old paper gets that distinct smell, kind of sweet and musty. 

But, uh, anyway... no, no major medical or neurological stuff. Just the broken wrist when I was little.

inference.note: No major medical/neurological history reported, which makes F06.2 less likely but does not rule it out; overall candidate list unchanged this turn.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed persecutory belief is held with delusional conviction versus longstanding suspicious personality traits by assessing insight into the possibility of being mistaken.
doctor.question: Do you think it is at all possible that you could be mistaken about the ensemble members undermining you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for almost two years I’ve been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I think I could be mistaken about the ensemble members undermining me, which directly addresses the fixed nature of my belief (delusions) and whether it can be changed or if I have insight into it being a delusion.

patient.answer:
Mistaken? I... I don't see how I could be. I mean, that's why I'm here, right? Because for almost two years now, I haven't been able to shake this absolute certainty about it. Ever since that big commission, a few of them have been doing it. Just quietly undermining my work. It's the schedule changes, the seating choices, the little comments during rehearsals. And I know they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away, but it doesn't change what I know is happening. 

It's like when you're tuning an orchestra, you know? The oboe plays the A, and everyone else is supposed to match it. But sometimes the strings will be just a fraction of a cent flat. Not enough for a casual listener to notice, but if you have a trained ear, it drives you absolutely crazy. It creates this subtle dissonance that just hangs in the air. I actually bought a new digital tuner last month because I thought my old one was losing its calibration. It's one of those strobe tuners, really precise. I ordered it from this specialty music shop in Chicago. I went to Chicago once for a conference, right in the middle of winter. The wind coming off Lake Michigan is no joke. I had to buy a new coat while I was there because the one I brought was completely useless. It was this heavy wool peacoat, navy blue. I still have it in my closet, actually, but I never wear it because it weighs like ten pounds and the buttons are loose. I tried to sew one back on, but I used the wrong color thread, so now it looks a bit ridiculous. 

But, um, anyway... no, I'm not mistaken. I know what they're doing, even if they try to cover it up with their little explanations.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed persecutory belief is bizarre/impossible rather than plausible, which best separates delusional disorder/paranoid personality from schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis.
doctor.question: Has anything about what these ensemble members are doing seemed impossible by ordinary means, like influencing you in ways normal people couldn't?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about bizarre delusions (whether the ensemble members' actions seem impossible by ordinary means, like mind control or telepathy), which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Impossible by ordinary means? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, they're just musicians, right? They're not doing anything supernatural or... or reading my mind. It's just normal, everyday sabotage. Missing cues, changing schedules, that kind of thing. 

Speaking of schedules, I actually bought a new planner recently to try and keep everything straight. It's one of those really nice leather-bound ones, you know? With the thick paper that doesn't bleed through when you use a fountain pen. I love fountain pens. I have this vintage Parker 51 that I found at an estate sale a few years ago. It took me forever to figure out how to clean the old dried ink out of the aerometric filler. I ended up watching like, three hours of YouTube tutorials on pen restoration. There's this whole community of people who just restore old pens. One guy had this amazing video where he fixed a cracked celluloid barrel using some kind of solvent welding technique. It was fascinating. I actually tried to buy some of the solvent he used, but you can't get it shipped to residential addresses anymore because it's apparently highly flammable. Probably for the best, honestly. I'd probably end up melting the pen entirely or setting my desk on fire. My desk is this old oak roll-top that I got from my grandfather, so I'd hate to ruin it. It has all these tiny little cubby holes that are completely useless for modern things, but they look great. 

But, uh, no... to answer your question, they aren't doing anything impossible. Just normal, frustrating things to undermine me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed persecutory belief is accompanied by prominent negative symptoms, which would help distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself becoming much less interested in people or activities you used to enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about negative symptoms (specifically anhedonia or social withdrawal / avolition), which are not covered by my symptom profile (which only includes delusions, functioning, functional impairment, and duration).

patient.answer:
Less interested? No, I don't think so. I mean, I still love music, obviously. I'm still composing, still trying to get my work out there despite... well, despite everything. I still enjoy reading, too. I just finished this incredible biography of Mahler. 

It's actually a really heavy book, physically, I mean. Hardcover, almost a thousand pages. I usually prefer reading on my tablet because it's easier to hold when I'm lying in bed, but the screen glare was starting to give me headaches. I went to the optometrist a few weeks ago to see if I needed a new prescription, but he said my eyes are fine. He suggested I try those blue-light blocking glasses. I bought a pair online, but they have these really thick, tortoiseshell frames that make me look like a 1950s librarian. I wore them to the grocery store once and the cashier kept giving me these weird looks. Or maybe it was because I bought like, six jars of artichoke hearts. They were on sale, and I was going to make this Mediterranean pasta salad I saw on a cooking show. The host of the show was this really energetic Italian guy who kept shouting at the camera. He made it look so easy, but when I tried it, the dressing split and it just looked like an oily mess. I ended up eating it anyway because I didn't want to waste the artichokes. They're surprisingly expensive when they're not on sale. 

But, um, anyway... no, I haven't lost interest in things. I still enjoy my usual hobbies and everything.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the delusional belief is accompanied by prominent mood episodes, which would help distinguish delusional disorder from schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: During these past two years, have you had a period when you felt very depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of depressed mood (feeling depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks) to rule out a depressive episode or mood disorder. The symptom profile does not contain an item related to depression or mood episodes.

patient.answer:
Depressed? No, no, I haven't had anything like that. I mean, I get frustrated with the ensemble, obviously, but not depressed. I don't really get down like that. Well, maybe a little gloomy when it rains for days on end, but that's just the weather. 

Actually, the last time it rained really heavily, my ceiling started leaking right over my piano. It's just a Yamaha upright, but I love the action on the keys. I had to scramble to put this orange plastic bucket on top of it to catch the water. The funny thing is, the sound of the water hitting the bottom of the bucket was pitching a perfect B-flat. Just... drip, drip, B-flat, B-flat. I actually pulled out my phone and recorded it to see if I could sample it for a piece I was working on. I use Logic Pro for my mixing, mostly. A lot of my friends swear by Ableton, but I just can't get used to the interface. It feels too blocky to me. I watched this masterclass by Hans Zimmer recently where he showed off his studio, and it is just wall-to-wall modular synthesizers. It looks like the bridge of a spaceship. I'd love to have a setup like that, but my apartment barely has enough room for a decent dining table. I usually end up eating dinner on my couch while watching nature documentaries. I saw this amazing one about cephalopods the other night. Did you know octopuses have three hearts? It's wild. They pump blue blood, too, because it's copper-based instead of iron. 

But, um... sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, feeling depressed. No, no periods of depression for me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are prominent thought-disorder/disorganization symptoms, which would help distinguish schizophrenia-spectrum disorders from persistent delusional or paranoid personality presentations.
doctor.question: Have other people ever said that your thoughts seem jumbled or that you jump from one idea to another in a way that is hard to follow?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about disorganized thinking or flight of ideas (symptoms of schizophrenia or mania). My profile only includes delusions, functioning not markedly impaired, functional impairment, and duration. It does not cover disorganized speech.

patient.answer:
Jumbled? No, I don't think anyone has ever told me that. I mean, my musicians complain about a lot of things, but usually it's about my tempos or the rehearsal schedule, not that I'm hard to follow. 

Speaking of rehearsal schedules, I was trying to coordinate a string quartet practice last week, and trying to get four musicians in the same room at the same time is like herding cats. I had to use this online scheduling poll thing, Doodle, I think it's called? But the cellist, David, he completely ignored it and just texted me a list of times he *couldn't* do, which is entirely unhelpful. David is a great player, don't get me wrong. He has this beautiful 19th-century French cello that just sings in the upper register. He bought it at an auction in Paris a few years ago. I've always wanted to go to Paris. I had a layover at Charles de Gaulle once, but I don't think that counts. The airport there is huge and confusing, honestly. I almost missed my connection to Berlin because I couldn't figure out which terminal I was supposed to be in. The signage was terrible, or maybe I was just sleep-deprived. I always get terrible jet lag when I fly east. I read somewhere that taking melatonin can help, but last time I tried it, I just had these incredibly vivid dreams about being trapped in a giant hourglass. Sand getting everywhere. It was awful. I ended up waking up at 3 AM and just eating cold pizza in my hotel room. 

But, uh, no, nobody's ever said my thoughts are jumbled. I think I'm pretty clear when I speak.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are prominent disorganized speech symptoms independent of the fixed persecutory belief, which would favor schizophrenia-spectrum disorders like schizophrenia or schizophreniform/brief psychosis over persistent delusional disorder or paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: Has anyone ever told you that, when you talk, you go off on tangents or lose track of the question?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about tangential speech or losing track of the question (a symptom of disorganized speech/thought). This is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile (Delusions, Additional Requirement 1, Functional Impairment, Duration).

patient.answer:
Go off on tangents? Lose track of the question? No, I don't think anyone's ever said that. I mean, I'm a director, I have to be pretty focused to keep everyone on the same page. 

Although, keeping people on the same page is literally impossible with sheet music these days. Half the ensemble uses iPads now, and they all have these Bluetooth page-turning pedals. It's supposed to be seamless, but during our last run-through, the second violinist's pedal disconnected right in the middle of a tricky allegro section. He had to stop playing to swipe the screen, and it totally ruined the momentum. I told him he should just go back to paper, but he says paper is bad for the environment. Which I get, I try to recycle as much as I can. I actually started composting recently, too. I got this little bin for my kitchen counter. It's supposed to be odor-free, but I put some onion skins in there last week and the whole apartment smelled like a deli for two days. I ended up having to buy this expensive citrus room spray to cover it up. The bottle said it was made with essential oils from the Amalfi coast. I love the smell of citrus, especially grapefruit. Have you ever tried a grapefruit brûlée? You cut it in half, sprinkle some sugar on top, and use a blowtorch to caramelize it. It's incredible. I got a kitchen torch for Christmas last year from my sister. She's a pastry chef in Chicago. Chicago is great, but the winters are just brutal. The wind off the lake goes right through your coat. 

But, um... wait, what were you asking about? Oh, tangents. No, no one's ever told me I do that. I usually get right to the point.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are persistent negative symptoms or marked social withdrawal outside the delusional belief, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from delusional disorder or paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: Have you been avoiding other people more than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about social withdrawal or avoiding other people (negative symptoms of schizophrenia or symptoms of depression), which is not covered by my symptom profile (Delusions, Additional Requirement 1, Functional Impairment, Duration).

patient.answer:
Avoiding people? No, not really. I mean, I have to be around people all the time for work. Rehearsals, meetings with venue managers, all that stuff. It's actually exhausting sometimes. 

Like yesterday, I had to meet with the lighting director for our upcoming performance at this old theater downtown. The place is gorgeous, all this ornate gold leafing and red velvet everywhere. It feels like stepping back into the 1920s. But the lighting rig is an absolute nightmare. It's half digital, half analog, and the guy running it kept complaining about the power draw. He was wearing this vintage leather jacket that squeaked every time he moved his arms. It was so distracting. I used to have a leather jacket like that in college, but I accidentally left it at a diner in Boston. We had gone there after a concert, and I ordered this massive plate of blueberry pancakes. Best pancakes I've ever had. I think the secret is they put a little bit of lemon zest in the batter. I tried making them at home once, but I totally messed up the ratio of baking powder and they came out flat as crepes. Crepes are good too, though, especially with Nutella and strawberries. I went to a crepe stand in Montreal once, and the guy making them was juggling the spatulas. It was like dinner and a show. 

But, uh, avoiding people? No, I'm pretty social. I don't really hide away or anything.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are formal thought disorder symptoms, specifically whether the patient can maintain goal-directed speech long enough to answer a simple direct question, which helps distinguish schizophrenia-spectrum disorders from delusional/paranoid personality presentations.
doctor.question: Can you tell me, in one sentence, why you think those ensemble members are undermining you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for almost two years I’ve been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about the core of my delusion (why I believe the ensemble members are undermining me), which corresponds to my symptom profile for Delusions.

patient.answer:
Well, you see, I'm here because for almost two years I've been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it. 

Which reminds me of this one email chain we had about the seating arrangement for the cellos. It was a complete disaster. The first chair cellist, Sarah, she insisted on being closer to the violas, saying it helped her hear the inner harmonies better. But I know she just wanted to be further away from the air conditioning vent. Those vents in the rehearsal hall are so loud, they sound like a jet engine taking off. Speaking of jet engines, I was watching this documentary the other day about how they test those things. They literally shoot frozen chickens into the turbines to simulate bird strikes. It's wild. I can't imagine being the person whose job it is to buy frozen chickens for that. Do they just go to a regular grocery store? I went to the store yesterday to get some chicken, actually, but they were completely out of thighs, which are the best part for roasting. I ended up getting breasts instead, but they always dry out so fast unless you brine them first. I have this great brine recipe with peppercorns and bay leaves. Bay leaves are funny, aren't they? You put them in, but you're not supposed to eat them. It feels like a trick. 

But anyway, yeah, that's why I think they're undermining me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the persistent persecutory belief is accompanied by first-rank/passivity phenomena, which would strongly favor schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis over delusional disorder or paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: Have you ever felt that your thoughts were being controlled by someone else?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thought control (thought insertion/broadcasting/control), which is a symptom of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders. This is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Controlled by someone else? Like mind control? No, I've never felt anything like that. My thoughts are my own. 

Though, sometimes I wish someone else could take over my thoughts just so I could get a break, you know? Especially when I'm trying to figure out the pacing for a new piece. I'll just lie in bed staring at the ceiling, trying to hear the transition from the woodwinds to the brass, and my brain just won't shut off. Speaking of brass, I had to take my French horn in for a cleaning last month. It's a vintage Conn 8D, beautiful instrument, but the valves get sticky if you don't oil them religiously. The repair guy I go to is this older gentleman who works out of his garage. His garage is amazing, it's packed floor to ceiling with instrument parts and old radios. He actually fixes antique radios as a hobby. He showed me this one from the 1930s that he restored, it had this gorgeous wooden cabinet with a glowing dial. It made me want to start listening to those old radio dramas, like The Shadow or something. I tried listening to a podcast once that was styled like an old radio show, but the voice acting was just so over the top I couldn't get into it. I mostly just listen to audiobooks now when I'm driving. I'm on this huge sci-fi kick right now. I just finished this book about a colony on Mars where they have to farm potatoes in their own... well, you know. It's fascinating how much science goes into making those stories believable. 

But no, my thoughts are definitely my own. No one's controlling them.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed persecutory belief is non-bizarre and isolated without other psychotic symptoms, helping distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum conditions.
doctor.question: Have you ever believed that ordinary events, comments, or messages were meant specifically for you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about ideas of reference (believing ordinary events/messages have special meaning specifically for the patient). My profile includes delusions of being undermined by ensemble members, but it does not specifically include ideas of reference as a separate symptom to report here.

patient.answer:
Meant specifically for me? Like hidden messages? No, I don't really think like that. I mean, I read reviews of our performances, and sometimes it feels like a critic is taking a personal swipe at my tempo choices, but that's just normal criticism, right? 

Speaking of reviews, there's this one local arts blogger who always has something to say about the percussion section. He's obsessed with the timpani. I actually ran into him at a coffee shop a few weeks ago. He was ordering this incredibly complicated matcha latte with oat milk and two pumps of vanilla. I don't get the whole matcha craze, honestly. It tastes like grass clippings to me. I prefer just a straight black coffee, maybe an espresso if I'm really dragging. I bought an espresso machine for my apartment last year, one of those shiny Italian ones. It took me a solid month to figure out how to pull a decent shot without burning the beans. You have to get the grind size exactly right, and the tamp pressure... it's practically a science experiment every morning. My neighbor actually complained about the noise of the grinder once. She's this sweet older lady who knits these tiny sweaters for her Chihuahua. The dog's name is Barnaby, and he barks at literally everything. A leaf blows across the sidewalk? Barnaby loses his mind. It's kind of hilarious, but also a little annoying when I'm trying to write a score. 

But yeah, no, I don't think random things are secretly meant for me. Just normal stuff.

doctor.intent: Distinguish a persistent single non-bizarre delusion with otherwise preserved functioning from schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis by testing for disorganized thought in the form of thought blocking.
doctor.question: Do your thoughts ever suddenly stop in the middle, as if your mind goes blank?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thought blocking (thoughts suddenly stopping or mind going blank), which is a symptom of schizophrenia or other thought disorders. This is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Stop in the middle? Like going completely blank? No, I haven't noticed anything like that. My brain is usually going a mile a minute, honestly. 

Though, I do get writer's block sometimes when I'm staring at a blank score. It's the absolute worst feeling, just looking at the empty staff paper. I actually have to use a very specific type of staff paper, it has to be this slightly off-white, almost cream color, because the bright white glares way too much under my desk lamp. My desk lamp is one of those vintage architect lamps with the adjustable spring arms. I found it at a thrift store for like ten bucks. It was a total steal, but I had to rewire the whole thing myself because the original cord was completely frayed and I really didn't want to start a fire. Speaking of fires, the fire alarm in my apartment building went off at 3 AM on Tuesday. Turns out someone on the fourth floor fell asleep while boiling eggs. Who boils eggs at 3 AM? And how do you even burn boiled eggs? All the water has to evaporate first. I usually soft-boil mine for exactly six and a half minutes, then drop them straight into an ice bath. It makes the shells peel off so easily. 

But anyway, what were we... oh, right. No, my thoughts don't just stop or go blank.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are persistent hallucinations in another sensory modality, which would favor schizophrenia-spectrum or organic psychosis over delusional disorder/paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: Have you ever seen things that other people could not see?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about visual hallucinations (seeing things that other people cannot see), which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Seen things? You mean like hallucinations or something? No, definitely not. I've got pretty good eyesight, actually. 

Though I did have to get new glasses a couple of months ago. My prescription barely changed, but I sat on my old frames by accident. I was in a rush to get to rehearsal and just flopped down on the couch without looking. They were these great tortoiseshell frames, too. I ended up getting wire-rimmed ones this time, kind of a retro look. The optometrist was this guy who wouldn't stop talking about his trip to Iceland. He spent like twenty minutes telling me about the hot springs and the puffins while he was shining that bright light in my eyes. I'd love to go to Iceland someday, maybe record some ambient soundscapes near the glaciers. I've been experimenting a lot with field recordings lately. I bought this portable Zoom recorder, and I just take it on walks and record random stuff—traffic, birds, the subway doors closing. I actually used a sample of a subway train braking in this experimental piece I wrote for a string quartet. The cellist hated it, she said it was too jarring, but that was exactly the point. I'm trying to push boundaries, you know? The classical music scene can be so rigid sometimes. If you don't write exactly like Mahler or Shostakovich, people look at you funny. I went to this concert last week where they played a piece entirely composed of silence and occasional coughing. It was... an experience. 

But no, I don't see things that aren't there. My vision is perfectly normal.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion lasting almost two years that ensemble members are subtly undermining his work, despite lack of confirmation and contrary explanations. There are no hallucinations, no thought control/insertion, no bizarre delusions, no sustained mood episodes, no clear negative symptoms, and no significant deterioration in functioning. Medical/neurological illness was denied, making persistent delusional disorder most consistent.
